title: Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: At life’s end, when all beings keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession, rebirth is attained.

inline.s: At life’s end, when all beings keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession, rebirth is attained.
Ten thoughts in unbroken succession — by constant practice they become second nature.
Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching
Biography of Master Daochuo — Vernacular
Biography of Master Daochuo — Original Text
Master Yinguang said:

“In the Tang dynasty there was Daochuo, who followed Tanluan’s teaching and devoted himself solely to Pure Land practice; throughout his life he lectured on the three Pure Land sutras nearly two hundred times. From Daochuo’s school there emerged Shandao
(the second patriarch of the Pure Land school)
, and after him Chengyuan
(the third patriarch)
, Fazhao
(the fourth patriarch)
, Shaokang
(the fifth patriarch)
, and Daxing; and so the lotus breeze spread far and wide within China and beyond.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
Letter to the Venerable Ti’an of Daxingshan Monastery)

Translation: In the Tang dynasty, Master Daochuo succeeded Master Tanluan and devoted himself solely to the Pure Land path. Throughout his life he lectured on the three Pure Land sutras nearly two hundred times. Many outstanding figures emerged from Master Daochuo’s school: Master Shandao (second patriarch of the Pure Land school), followed by Master Chengyuan (third patriarch), Master Fazhao (fourth patriarch), Master Shaokang (fifth patriarch), and Master Daxing. Thus the lotus breeze of the Pure Land school flourished within China and beyond.

[Daxing] Shi Daxing was a native of Qizhou. He later entered Mount Tai, where he made his clothing of grass and lived on wild plants and bark. Practicing the Lotus Samādhi, he moved Samantabhadra to appear before him. He sighed to himself: ‘Life is impermanent and must end in dissolution; who knows in what realm I shall be reborn in the next life?’ He then entered the scripture treasury and, taking up a sutra at random, obtained the teaching of the Western Land. He then fixed his mind single-mindedly on Amitābha Buddha; during the third week of seven days (three sevens — twenty-one days), in the middle of the night, he suddenly beheld a ground of lapis lazuli. His mind’s eye opened wide, and he saw the Buddhas of the ten directions, like images in a bright mirror. Later the emperor summoned Daxing into the inner palace, lodged him in the imperial hall, and conferred on him the title ‘Ever-Vigorous Bodhisattva,’ making him a founding duke. A year later he showed a slight illness and passed away lying on his right side (the lion posture). After burial, when his coffin was opened, his appearance was seen to be as in life, and a rare fragrance lingered. (From the Song Biographies of Eminent Monks)

Master Daochuo was the teacher of Master Shandao. He was versed alike in doctrinal study, Chan, and Pure Land practice, and his attainments were extremely high (see the biography that follows). He gave a series of incisive teachings on Pure Land cultivation, which serve as a guide for students of the Pure Land school. Excerpts with commentary are given below:
Concerning the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow (the vow of ten thoughts ensuring birth) among Amitābha Buddha’s forty-eight vows, Master Daochuo clearly explains in the Anle Ji:
“If there are beings who, though they have spent a whole life committing evil,
at the hour of death keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession
and call my name — if they are not born, I will not attain perfect enlightenment.”
[The Eighteenth Vow]

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who with sincere hearts rejoice and believe, and who wish to be born in my land, should even down to ten thoughts fail to be born — may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Excepted are those who commit the five grave offenses or slander the true Dharma.”
(From the Sutra of the Buddha of Infinite Life)
Here Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of “down to ten thoughts” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the hour of death, ten thoughts in unbroken succession.
Therefore the “down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow refers to the ten thoughts at the hour of death, and moreover to ten thoughts kept in unbroken succession.
Concerning
ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end bringing immediate birth, Master Daochuo teaches in the Anle Ji:
At the hour of death for all beings
, the knife-wind rends the body apart, the suffering of death presses in, and great terror arises. Therefore, meeting a good spiritual friend and rousing great valor,
keeping ten thoughts in unbroken succession
is a supreme good root, and
rebirth is thereby attained
Here Master Daochuo teaches: at the hour of death, if all beings keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession, rebirth is attained. That is to say:
ten thoughts at life’s end, in unbroken succession, bring immediate birth.

[Knife-wind] When a person is on the verge of death, the four great elements disintegrate and the suffering of death is endured. The wind that severs the limbs and joints like knives is called the “knife-wind.” The Sutra of Right Mindfulness says: “When the end of life is seen, the knife-wind stirs throughout; skin, flesh, sinews, and bones; fat, marrow, essence, and blood — all are cut and divided.” The Sutra of the Five Kings says: “When death is near, the knife-wind rends the form apart; there is no place without pain.”
Concerning
the ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end, Master Daochuo has another extremely important teaching in the Anle Ji, transcribed and annotated below:

[Question: The Great Sutra of Infinite Life says: ‘The beings of the ten directions who with sincere hearts rejoice and believe, and who wish to be born in my land, should even down to ten thoughts fail to be born — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.’ Now there are people in the world who, having heard this sacred teaching, give it no attention at all in their present life. They plan to wait until the hour of death before beginning to practice the recitation. What of this matter?]

Question: The Sutra of Infinite Life says: ‘The beings of the ten directions who with sincere hearts rejoice and believe, and who wish to be born in my land, should even down to ten thoughts fail to be born — may I not attain perfect enlightenment.’ There are some who, on hearing this sacred teaching, pay it no heed whatsoever, planning to wait until the hour of death before accomplishing ten unbroken thoughts. What is one to make of such a plan?
[Answer: This matter is not of the same kind. Why? The sutra says ‘
ten thoughts in unbroken succession

’, which seems not difficult. But ordinary beings’ minds are like wild horses, their consciousness more restless than monkeys, galloping among the six sense-objects without a moment’s rest. Each must rouse faith and
in advance train the mind, so that repeated practice becomes second nature

and the good root grows firm. As the Buddha told the great king: ‘One who has stored up good deeds meets death without evil thoughts; as a tree already leaning will surely fall in the direction it inclines.’ If the knife-wind suddenly arrives and a hundred sufferings assail the body, and the habit has not been formed beforehand, how can the intended mindfulness be
(accomplished)

Answer: Such a plan is to dig a well when already thirsty. Digging a well when thirsty and building a bridge beforehand are two entirely different matters (“this matter is not of the same kind”). Why? The sutra says ‘ten thoughts in unbroken succession,’ which seems not difficult (so many suppose they will be able to do it at life’s end). Yet all ordinary beings’ minds are like wild horses, their consciousness more restless than monkeys, galloping among the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects) without a moment’s rest. Each person must rouse single-minded faith and, beforehand, train the mind to single-pointedness and ten unbroken thoughts, so that repeated practice becomes second nature (through constant practice, making single-pointed mindfulness and ten unbroken thoughts instinctive), and at life’s end the good root may stand firm. As the Buddha told the great king: ‘If one constantly stores up good deeds in ordinary times, then at death there will be no evil thoughts; just as when a tree falls, it will surely fall in the direction it already leans.’ If the knife-wind of death suddenly arrives and a hundred sufferings press in, and one has not beforehand made ten unbroken thoughts second nature, how could one possibly accomplish ‘ten unbroken thoughts’ at the hour of death merely by wishing to?

[Prepare a bridge beforehand] “Jinliang” means a ford and a bridge; “to prepare a ford and bridge beforehand” means to make ready in advance. [Consciousness more restless than monkeys] The six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness) churn even more violently than leaping, capering monkeys. [Repeated practice becomes second nature] Through repeated practice, making something instinctive.

[Each of you should, with three or five like-minded companions, agree beforehand to take turns enlightening and exhorting one another at the hour of death, reciting the name of Amitābha and wishing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, so that recitation follows recitation and ten thoughts are completed. It is like pressing a wax seal into clay: when the seal melts, the design is formed. The moment this life ends is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once entering the assembly of the definitely settled, what further worry could there be? Each of you should weigh this great benefit — why not train the mind beforehand?]

Therefore, it is best to invite three or five like-minded companions and agree in advance: at the hour of death, they will take turns enlightening and exhorting the dying person, reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha for them, encouraging them to hold firm their aspiration for rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, recitation following recitation, so that they accomplish ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end. It is like
pressing a carved wax seal into a clay mold: when heated, the wax seal melts, yet the pattern impressed on the clay has already taken shape;

therefore the moment the breath ceases (the seal melts) is the moment of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (the design is formed). Upon reaching the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one immediately enters the assembly of the definitely settled — what further worry could there be then? Each of you must weigh this immense benefit: why not train the ten unbroken thoughts beforehand?
[Successively] In unbroken succession.

[Wax seal pressed into clay; when the seal melts, the design is formed] A wax seal carved with a pattern is pressed into a clay mold. When the mold is heated and dried, the wax seal melts, while the pattern impressed on the clay is formed. The clay mold is the mold used to cast metal vessels. The Nirvana Sutra says:
“As a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal joins with the clay; when the seal perishes, the design is formed.”

Master Daochuo’s use here of “wax seal pressed into clay; when the seal melts, the design is formed” is a metaphor: we use this physical body to practice; if we accomplish ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end, then when the breath stops, the physical body dies (the seal melts), yet the great matter of rebirth is accomplished at that very moment (the design is formed) — “the moment this life ends is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”

[Assembly of the definitely settled] One of the three groups. [Three groups] The three groups are three classes of beings: the group of the definitely settled, the group of the definitely unsettled, and the indeterminate group. The group of the definitely settled refers to those beings who are certain to awaken; the group of the definitely unsettled to those who ultimately cannot awaken; and the indeterminate group to those who fall between the two, who may or may not awaken.
[Why not train the mind beforehand?] Why not practice the ten unbroken thoughts beforehand? This is what Master Yongming, who was Amitābha Buddha returned, said:
“If you wish to accomplish ten thoughts at life’s end, prepare the ford and bridge beforehand.”
(From the Wanshan Tonggui Ji) [Accomplish ten thoughts at life’s end] To accomplish ten unbroken thoughts at the hour of death. Master Yongming teaches:
“When walking the path
(circumambulating)
and paying homage, when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, be earnest, toiling, and sincere,
free of all other thoughts
, as if facing execution, as if in prison
(bi lao: a prison)

, pursued by robbers and enemies, pressed by water and fire, single-mindedly seeking rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly to realize non-arising, broadly to deliver sentient beings, to uphold and exalt the Three Jewels, vowing to repay the four kinds of kindness. With such sincerity, it will surely not be in vain. If words and deeds do not match, if the power of faith is slight, lacking
the mind of thought following thought in unbroken succession

, but having the intention of repeated interruptions, and relying on such indolence one hopes for birth at life’s end — then, only obstructed by karmic hindrances, one will likely fail to meet such good friends, and pressed by wind and fire, right mindfulness will not be achieved. Why?
The present is the cause, the hour of death the result
; the cause must be genuine, and then the result will not be empty. If you wish to
accomplish ten thoughts at life’s end
, merely prepare the ford and bridge beforehand, gather together merit and dedicate it to that moment, so that thought after thought is not deficient — and there will be nothing to worry about.”
(From the Wanshan Tonggui Ji) [Prepare the ford and bridge] “Jinliang” means a ford and a bridge; “to prepare the ford and bridge” means to make ready in advance.
In the Anle Ji, Master Daochuo also gives two extremely important teachings on Buddha-recitation and rebirth:
[Even if one has spent a whole life committing evil,
if one can fix the mind with single-pointed devotion
and constantly recite the Buddha’s name, all hindrances will naturally dissolve and rebirth is assured.]
This passage means: even though one has been committing evil,
after one repents
, if one can
fix the mind with single-pointed devotion
(pure thoughts in succession) and constantly recite the Buddha’s name, then all hindrances naturally dissolve and rebirth is assured.

Please note: “even if one has spent a whole life committing evil” describes the state before repentance; “if one can fix the mind with single-pointed devotion and constantly recite the Buddha’s name” describes the state after repentance. For if one had not truly repented, how could one fix the mind with single-pointed devotion?

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all without exception attain birth. Upon reaching that land, one enters the assembly of the definitely settled, equal in merit to ten thousand kalpas of practice on this path.]

From the utmost of a whole life of thought following thought in unbroken succession, down to ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end, all attain birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon reaching the Western Land, one enters the assembly of the definitely settled, equal in efficacy to ten thousand kalpas of practice through the ordinary path!

[From the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts] Judging from the Anle Ji as a whole, the meaning is: from the utmost of a whole life of thought following thought in unbroken succession, down to ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end. The ancients prized brevity in writing, so when interpreting, one must always read the preceding and following passages together; never take a phrase literally in isolation or quote out of context.

We read the sutras and the treatises and teachings of the patriarchs and great masters all in order to seek the truth. Therefore, one must act from a truthful heart: things are as they are, and one should take them as they are. Never, for the sake of private ends and private gain, play the game of quoting out of context — for example, twisting “from the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all without exception attain birth” into: “Master Daochuo said that as long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times (‘down to ten thoughts’), one will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at death (‘all without exception attain birth’). Therefore, reciting the name guarantees birth.” The fact is that before “from the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all without exception attain birth,” Master Daochuo has already clearly stated:
at the hour of death, ten thoughts in unbroken succession, calling my name
if one can fix the mind with single-pointed devotion
(pure thoughts in succession)
, and constantly recite the Buddha’s name

”, and so forth. Therefore, reading the preceding and following passages together, “down to ten thoughts” means ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end, not ten scattered recitations in ordinary times. Quoting out of context in this way not only misleads others but also harms oneself.
In the Anle Ji, Master Daochuo further teaches:

[Exhort all beings to keep mindfulness ever present. A verse says: When in one’s prime and free from affliction, one is indolent and does not strive; greedily pursuing many affairs, one does not cultivate giving, precepts, or meditation. Only when death is about to swallow one up does one regret and seek to cultivate good. The wise should observe and cut off thoughts of the five desires. One who diligently trains the mind has no regret at life’s end; when the mind has become single-pointed, there are no confused thoughts.
The wise diligently gather the mind, and at life’s end the mind does not scatter. One who has not trained the mind to single-pointedness will surely be scattered at life’s end.
When the mind is scattered, it is like a horse trained only to turn a millstone: in battle it will only circle and cannot run straight.]

Exhort all beings to keep mindfulness ever present. The verse says: if, in the vigor of youth, one is indolent and does not strive, greedily pursuing all manner of affairs and failing to cultivate giving, precepts, and meditation, then when death is about to swallow one up, it will be too late to repent and wish to cultivate good (here “good” refers to the “giving, precepts, and meditation” mentioned above — generosity, moral discipline, and meditative concentration). The wise should observe their own minds well, in order to cut off the delusions of the five desires. One who thus diligently trains the mind to single-pointedness has no regret at life’s end, because, the mind having already become single-pointed through habituation, there will be no confused thoughts at the hour of death. The wise, because they diligently gather the mind in ordinary times, will not let the mind scatter at life’s end (thus accomplishing right mindfulness at death and attaining rebirth). But one who does not train the mind to single-pointedness in ordinary times will surely be scattered at life’s end (thus failing to accomplish right mindfulness at death and continuing to revolve in the six realms). When the mind is scattered at that moment, one cannot make it single-pointed even if one wishes — just as a horse trained only to turn a millstone will, in battle, only circle and cannot run straight.

[Five desires] Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form refers to beautiful appearances; sound to melodious voices; smell to fragrant scents; taste to delicious flavors; touch to pleasurable sensations. Because these five can give rise to greed, they are called the five desires. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching, the Buddha says:
“You should restrain the five faculties
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, body)
, and not let them run loose into the five desires.”
[Like a horse trained to turn a millstone] Like using the turning of a millstone to train a horse. “Wei (wèi)” means a millstone.
(The original text appears in the Records of Pure Land Sages)

Master Daochuo, secular surname Wei, was a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou (present-day Taiyuan, Shanxi). At fourteen he left home and devoted himself to the study of doctrine and the treatises; he also studied Chan under the Chan master Huizan. Later he dwelt at Xuanzhong Monastery in Shibi Valley, Wenshui, a place of practice founded by Master Tanluan. Master Daochuo greatly admired Master Tanluan’s achievements in Pure Land practice, and so he single-mindedly contemplated Amitābha Buddha and the Land of Ultimate Bliss with a settled mind. When sitting, he always faced west; throughout the six periods of the day he paid homage to Amitābha Buddha at the appointed times without omission, and he made reciting the Buddha’s name seventy thousand times his daily fixed practice. Other monks, in meditation, personally saw auspicious signs of the Western Pure Land, and saw Master Daochuo holding his rosary, his whole body a vivid red, tall as a mountain of the seven jewels; there were yet other auspicious responses too numerous to relate in full.

Master Daochuo lectured for the assembly on the Sutra of Infinite Life and the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Infinite Life nearly two hundred times. All who came to listen held their rosaries and recited the Buddha’s name, and the sound of recitation swelled like the tide and the waves. When the lecture ended and the assembly dispersed, the sound of recitation rang through the mountain forests and valleys. Master Daochuo constantly encouraged and urged beings to practice the Pure Land path, and his exposition was penetrating and lucid, welling forth like a clear spring. He often urged people to draw in their thoughts, cease their clinging, and single-mindedly recollect and recite the Buddha’s name. He composed the Anle Ji in two fascicles, which in its broad reach encompasses the thought of the two bodhisattvas Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, and in its nearer scope connects with the writings of Huiyuan and Tanluan. Its words and principles strike to the heart of the matter, and it was esteemed and honored by the people of his time.

In the second year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong of Tang (628), during a group practice session, the assembly all saw Master Tanluan seated on a boat of the seven jewels, saying to Master Daochuo: ‘Because of your vigorous practice, the palace and pavilions that are the reward of your merits in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are already complete; it is only that you still have some worldly conditions to exhaust.’ At the same time they saw transformation Buddhas filling the sky, and all manner of wondrous heavenly flowers drifting down from the void. The whole assembly gazed upward with joy and unceasingly praised the wonder of it. From that time on, the vigor of Master Daochuo’s body, won through his assiduous practice, grew ever stronger, and his complexion shone ever more brightly. Monastics and laypeople alike, drawn by his fame, came to him in ever-growing numbers, until at last, past the age of eighty, he passed away.

There was at that time a monk named Shi Daofu, who shared Master Daochuo’s aspiration for birth in the Pure Land. Whenever the two met, they pledged one another to be born together in the Pure Land. Three days after Master Daochuo passed away, Daofu heard the news and said: ‘I had always hoped to go first; who would have thought that now I would be behind? Let me exert just a little more strength, and I can follow Daochuo.’ Thereupon, before the Buddha image, he bowed his head, made his vows, then withdrew to his seat and passed away.
(From the Records of Pure Land Sages)
Tang
Daochuo and Daofu

Daochuo, surname Wei, was a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou. At fourteen he left home and studied the sutras and treatises, and also attended the Chan master Zan to study Chan. Later he dwelt at Xuanzhong Monastery in Shibi Valley, Wenshui, which had been founded by the Dharma master Tanluan. Daochuo admired Tanluan’s Pure Land work, and so he devoted himself to contemplation, always sitting facing west, never missing his homage through the six periods of the day, and reciting the Buddha’s name to the count of seventy thousand each day. A monk in meditation beheld an auspicious sign of the West, and saw Daochuo holding his rosary, crimson like a mountain of the seven jewels. His other auspicious responses cannot be fully described. Daochuo lectured for the assembly on the Sutra of Infinite Life and the Contemplation Sutra nearly two hundred times. Those who heard him each clutched their beads and recited the Buddha’s name, like the sound of the tide; and when the assembly dispersed, the sound filled the woods and valleys. In ordinary times he spurred on the Pure Land work, his eloquence welling up like a spring, urging people to gather their thoughts, quiet their clinging, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. He wrote the Pure Land Treatise in two fascicles, encompassing Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, and reaching down to the writings of Huiyuan and Tanluan; its words and purport are incisive and essential, and his contemporaries held it in high regard. In the second year of Zhenguan, the assembly saw Master Luan seated on a boat of the seven jewels, who said to Daochuo: ‘Your Pure Land halls are complete; it is only that your remaining retribution is not yet exhausted.’ They also saw transformation Buddhas dwelling in the sky, with heavenly flowers drifting down, and the assembly all rejoiced and marveled. From then on Daochuo’s retributive vigor grew ever stronger, his complexion flourished, and those who turned to him, monastic and lay, grew daily. At over eighty he passed away. There was at that time a monk named Shi Daofu, of the same aspiration as Daochuo; whenever they met, they pointed to the Pure Land as their appointed meeting. Three days after Daochuo died, Daofu heard of it and said: ‘I had always expected to go first; now I am behind. Let me add one breath’s effort, and I can catch up with him.’ Before the Buddha image he bowed his head, made his vow, withdrew to his seat, and passed away.
